editor_spans.body: Read in order, the government's statements on Ukraine this week show that the energy ceasefire is about energy prices at home as much as it is about Ukraine. The first reaction to the US–Russia agreement of 9 October gave as much space to energy markets and the cost of living as to Ukraine. The Prime Minister then told the Commons that an energy ceasefire is 'the quickest way' to get diesel back onto world markets. Britain's lines on 'just and lasting peace' are about principle, but its interest in a ceasefire is the price of fuel.

This produces a tension that none of the announcements admits. London wants Russian-linked energy flowing back into world markets to bring prices down. In the same week, the Chancellor is asking partners at the IMF to copy Britain's ban on Russian LNG shipping and to 'curtail the war chest'. Within days, the ceasefire the Prime Minister welcomed had become a list of Russian strikes on energy infrastructure 'since President Trump called for' it. Britain's answer was more missiles and more sanctions. The government is relying on Washington to deliver lower energy prices while it supplies the pressure on Russia itself. Each time that pressure is stepped up, the ceasefire Britain is counting on looks less likely to hold.

The 9 October statement is also notable for what it leaves out. It never says what the US and Russia agreed. It opens by insisting that 'the UK's position could not be clearer' and ends by pledging full support for 'US-led efforts'. That is how a government sounds when it is reacting to a deal made without it. Zelenskyy's visit to Downing Street and the extra packages that followed look like Britain trying to show it still matters on a peace process that Washington is running.

In two announcements a day apart, the Prime Minister is doing two opposite things. In Lanarkshire he argues that power 'was never supposed to stop at the doors' of Holyrood and calls the Scottish Government one of Europe's most centralised. The day before, he presented Great British Railways as a single national body that brings the railway 'together around one mission', run from one headquarters. These are not principles applied the same way everywhere. Centralisation is offered where Westminster controls the service. Devolving power below the national level is urged on the one government run by a rival party.

The Scottish offer goes through No10 North and the Scotland Office. In other words, the UK government would help shape how power is handed out inside Scotland, which is devolved ground. The offer may be 'genuine', as the Scottish Secretary says. Even so, it gives Westminster a route to regions and cities that bypasses Holyrood. It is also a pitch to Scottish voters about who is the real centraliser.

The Derby timetable matters more than the opening ceremony will. Building at Becketwell begins in early 2027 and is due to finish by spring 2029, around the latest date the next general election can be held. The 600 apprenticeships over four years are small against a workforce where under 7% are under 25. The early successes the government claims for public ownership (frozen fares, extra seats) are things it can undo easily. The headquarters is meant to make the change permanent, but it will not be finished until a new government could be in office.
